items.originalTitle: Poll: Midterm losses deepen divide between MAGA and non-MAGA Trump voters
items.author: Erin Doherty
items.title: Poll: Midterm losses deepen divide between MAGA and non-MAGA Trump voters
items.summary: The Republican Party’s midterm wipeout has torn apart President Donald Trump’s coalition. For months, polling has shown cracks among Trump’s 2024 voters over immigration , the Iran war and the president’s influence. Now, new results from The POLITICO Poll , conducted just days after the election, reveal a deep chasm between Trump’s self-identified MAGA base and the non-MAGA voters who helped fuel his return to the White House. The two camps hold sharply different interpretations of the GOP’s historic midterm defeat and what comes next for their party, according to the survey conducted by PF Global. MAGA Trump loyalists were more likely to say the president is not to blame for the losses — that things would have gone better if he was on the ballot — and that the party should now move closer to Trump. Non-MAGA Trump voters starkly disagreed, saying they are ready to move away from him and his unpopular agenda. About one in five said they voted for Democratic candidates this cycle. The fault line is a fresh warning sign that Republicans, desperate to stitch back together a winning coalition after their midterm calamity, may struggle to keep the voters that powered Trump’s victory in 2024 in the fold. And it calls into question just how loyal the party should be to a leader — and movement — it has spent the last decade united around. Overall, just over half of all Trump voters said the president will be able to make a comeback from the election losses. “As the [GOP] spends the next two years figuring out who it is and what it stands for, these divisions will only be further exposed,” said Republican strategist Doug Heye. Here are four charts that show just how much the midterms have divided Trump’s own voters. A majority of non-MAGA Trump voters blamed Republicans' loss of the House and the Senate on Trump’s actions since taking office, with far fewer saying the campaigns themselves were responsible. A 59% majority also said the president is a loser of the midterms, a striking rebuke from a group of voters who helped his return to the White House. But MAGA Trump voters are torn over who they blame for their losses. The divide mirrors disagreements happening at the top levels of the Republican Party. In the immediate aftermath of the election, some Republicans, at least tepidly, began pointing fingers at the president. Others have called for a “reckoning” without explicitly laying the blame at Trump’s feet or articulating an alternative vision for the GOP. “There is no way to sugarcoat what happened on Election Day. From coast to coast, and in some of the reddest parts of the country, Republicans were humiliated,” 31 Republican National Committee members wrote in a letter to GOP lawmakers this week. Trump, who ahead of the midterms repeatedly urged voters to “pretend” he was on the ballot, insisted in a Truth Social post after the election that, “I JUST WASN’T ON THE BALLOT. IF I WERE, WE WOULD HAVE WON IN A LANDSLIDE!” “President Trump will never stop delivering results for the American people and he will undoubtedly go down as the most successful and consequential president in American history,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. As Republican Party leaders grapple with how to rebound from the midterms, MAGA isn’t ready to move on from Trump: They said the path forward is embracing Trump and his agenda. Non-MAGA Trump voters said the opposite — and nearly half of them think their Republican candidates should have broken with the president on the economy this cycle. “It is very clear that Election Day 2026 was an unequivocal rebuke of Donald Trump, both him personally and his policies,” said one national GOP operative who worked on midterm races, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the landscape. “MAGA needs a serious rebrand if it is going to have any success in the future.” That presents a complicated picture for Republican leaders, who will have to find a way to appeal to Trump’s fiercely loyal MAGA base without alienating the less committed voters who helped deliver his 2024 victory. On Election Night, as the scale of Republican losses was becoming clear, POLITICO asked GOP operatives who worked on midterm races whether the defeat meant it was time for Republicans to consider a new vision for the party. “How can it not be?” one person responded. It’s “the worst defeat a party has taken in 50 years.” Non-MAGA Trump voters are split over whether Trump can make a comeback after the midterms bloodbath. MAGA, however, is quite confident in the president’s abilities to do so. And collectively, Trump voters are more optimistic about the Republican Party than the president. Some key aspects of Trump’s agenda are unpopular with Americans, including his push for mass deportations, tariffs imposed on key trade partners and the war in Iran. The congressional Republicans who once supported many of those policies are now weighing whether they can distance themselves to regain voters’ trust. In an interview with “ 60 Minutes ” after the midterms, Trump admitted his party’s losses may be attributed at least in part to the Iran war and the resulting high gas prices — though he also mentioned how, in some cases, voters “didn’t like the candidates” and asserted, again, that he wasn’t on the ballot. "President Trump remains the unequivocal leader of our party who's cut taxes, lowered drug costs and secured our border,” RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said in a statement. “Republicans will continue to harness his ability to energize our base and expose the Democrats' disastrous record to win back our majorities in 2028." As the party looks ahead to 2028, Republicans are already weighing how much the party’s next presidential nominee should carry the MAGA mantle. Some Hill Republicans are increasingly warming to the prospect of a Marco Rubio presidential bid, arguing that voters may be looking for a new direction after Trump — and Vice President JD Vance may be too closely tied to the president’s agenda. MAGA Trump voters said decisively that they prefer someone who has worked in the administration — another sign of their support for the president, and of the difficulty of changing course as a party given that loyalty. “I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern recently told POLITICO . Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”

items.summary: LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy . If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off) , respectively. LG B6E OLED TV Where to Buy: $1399.99 $699.99 at Best Buy (55-inch) $1899.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $2699.99 $1499.99 at Best Buy (77-inch) Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 , the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform. The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

items.author: Carole Edmunds as told to Katie Cunningham
items.title: Kindness of strangers: I was stranded, dressed as a flapper, on a freezing night. Then a cheerful taxi driver pulled over
items.summary: My tyre was blown so he changed it for me. When I offered payment, he said ‘Don’t be ridiculous love’ Read more in the kindness of strangers series I had to fight not to lose control of the car. I was in my early 20s and driving home from a fancy dress party when bang – my tyre suddenly blew. I managed to wrestle my Toyota Corolla to a stop without crashing and sat there, heart pounding, as I wondered what to do next. It was 1982 in Canberra; a foggy, bitterly cold night in the middle of winter. I was wearing a silly flapper dress and high heels – I’m not sure I’d even packed a jacket! I had a spare tyre in the back, but little idea how to change it. My options were to make the one hour walk home alone or wait to see if another car passed and could offer me a ride. For 30 minutes I sat in the driver’s seat helplessly, unsure what to do.

items.originalTitle: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.author: Judy Berman
items.title: All Hail Philomena Cunk, the Perfect Fake Newswoman for Our Age of Ignorance
items.summary: Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix In the future, when some documentary series in whatever medium succeeds television looks back at the current decade in public discourse, it might name our era the Age of Ignorance. The crank shouting nonsense from atop a soapbox is, of course, nothing new. What’s unique to our time is how vast the audiences for these bloviators have become. We’ve got Alix Earle , with about 15 million followers across TikTok and Instagram, bragging about never having read a book. (Even if it wasn’t strictly true, how telling that she would let us believe it.) We’ve got Joe Rogan , by many measures the most popular podcaster out there—a guy who has platformed pandemic misinformation and had to apologize for using racial slurs — influencing nationwide elections . Just last week , Fox News star turned YouTuber Tucker Carlson entertained the possibility that the Smithsonian is suppressing evidence of the existence of Goliath-like giants. To which Philomena Cunk says: “Hold my snake oil.” The world-famous British TV presenter described by the Guardian as “ iconically stupid ” is back on Netflix and BBC Two with Cunk on Cinema , a six-part docuseries in which she gripes that reading subtitles makes it impossible to concentrate on one’s phone and pronounces D.W. Griffith’s KKK mash note The Birth of a Nation a “typically woke Hollywood fantasy.” (In what may or may not be a nod to viewers’ short attention spans, episodes top out at 15 minutes and can be binged in less time than it takes to watch most films.) Cunk is so incompetent, it’s hilarious. But unlike the personalities listed above, she’s meant to be funny—because she is a fictional character played by Diane Morgan. And although she was conceived when Earle was a tween and Carlson had bosses to answer to, she has since become the perfect fake newswoman to send up our Age of Ignorance. She may not be a real human being, but Cunk has had the kind of rise broadcast journalists dream about. After making her name in 2013 as an astonishingly dim yet opinionated commentator on Black Mirror creator Charlie Brooker ’s BBC Two comedy news show Weekly Wipe , she leveled up to hosting mockumentaries like Cunk on Shakespeare and Cunk on Britain , all helmed by Brooker. Like the other thought leaders we trust to guide us through complex topics on screen, in her solo efforts, Cunk combines her own explanations and analyses (“If the Tudors were the Kardashians of their time, this was their Kim: Henry of Eight”) with real expert interviews. “How important are the words in a Shakespeares [sic] play?” she once asked the venerable Shakespearean actor Simon Russell Beale. “Could you do it without the words?” In early 2023, she broke UK containment, arriving on Netflix with her own, let’s say, unique, series-length take on world history, Cunk on Earth . Two years later, her special Cunk on Life dared to ask big questions about nature and the universe—the implicit one being: What would Planet Earth be like if Sir David Attenborough had the intellect of a microorganism? Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Philomena Cunk is a very British creation, in the tradition of Steve Coogan’s boorish TV-presenter character Alan Partridge and Sacha Baron Cohen ’s Da Ali G Show alter egos. From SNL ’s “Weekend Update” to The Daily Show , America’s news-satire tradition favors comedians telling dark jokes about current events in their own voices. But by the time she crossed the Atlantic, three years ago, U.S. audiences were primed to make Cunk a cult-comedy hero stateside, circulating her quotes and searching YouTube for morsels of her earlier work. Cunk on Life even scored a pair of Emmy nominations . It’s true that Baron Cohen broke out bigger in the U.S., during the 2000s, especially with his ingenuously inappropriate Kazakh reporter character, Borat. But his heyday coincided with a golden age of confrontational political satire, when Michael Moore broke box office records with documentaries built around interviews that embarrassed conservative icons like Charlton Heston and culture jammers like the Yes Men captured their elaborate anti-corporate hoaxes in feature films. Baron Cohen did something similar. As Baron Cohen wrote in an essay for TIME that coincided with the October release of his feature Ali G: Who Iz I? : “Each of my characters has a specific mechanism to encourage people to drop their guards and show what they really believe, prejudices and all.” In one notorious Ali G Show stunt, Borat got the patrons of an Arizona honky-tonk singing and clapping along to a song about throwing Jews down a well (though some later said they were behaving as directed or always knew it was all a bit). Morgan has a different agenda. She rarely humiliates the experts she interviews, who are generally in on the joke but, as in real news programs, aren’t given the questions in advance. Sure, she does occasionally mystify someone. In Cunk on Cinema , that person is Michael Bay , who at one point exclaims: “These are odd questions!” Most of the time, Cunk only embarrasses herself, though she’s too dim to realize it. The cringe comedy comes from the way the character makes the leading minds in every field behave as though the idiotic non sequiturs she imposes on them are worth engaging with. They’re too polite (or leery of coming off as elitists) not to. And when they do ever-so-gently push back, she tends to perform offendedness. “What was the Soviet Onion?” she asks a history professor in Cunk on Earth . She must mean the Soviet Union, he replies. “I don’t wanna be rude,” Cunk counters, despite much evidence to the contrary, “but I think you’re mansplaining a bit.” As Brooker has said : “The strange thing about Cunk is she’s sort of weirdly in charge of things, even if she’s speaking to a professor or whatever.” Diane Morgan in Cunk on Cinema —Netflix Between interviews, she pontificates in the tones of a veteran newsreader, albeit one who has no understanding of the subject on which she’s been asked to extemporize. Cunk on Cinema will be extra entertaining to anyone who’s ever read a book or taken a survey course on the history of film, because of how deftly it plays on the field’s tropes and touchstones. Stanley Kubrick ca. 2001: A Space Odyssey is described offhandedly as a “groovy young director.” She refers to Soviet montage master Sergei Eisenstein’s landmark silent film Battleship Potemkin as Batsh-t Pumpkin , “one of cinema’s unwatchable masterpieces.” You needn’t have a Ph.D in Cinema Studies to appreciate the humor Brooker and Morgan wring out of Cunk’s hopelessness with names and titles. Wayne John, Marlo Brandon, E Dot T Dot (a.k.a. E.T. ). Quentin Tarantino , she informs us, “is Italian for five spiders.” If you’ve ever listened to a TikToker with no medical training evangelize unregulated peptide injections, you’ll see mirrored in Cunk the blithe confidence of a person who’s getting rich repackaging their ignorance as subversive truth-telling. When she wonders, “Was James Dean born a teenager?,” it’s a benign version of the level of question we typically get from podcast hosts who spend three-hour episodes credulously “hearing out” conspiracy theorists. Now, as you might expect from a writing team led by the Black Mirror guy, she’s got artificial intelligence to hallucinate along with her. In Cunk on Cinema , she insists to Die Hard screenwriter Steven E. de Souza that the all-American genius of silent comedy Buster Keaton spoke in a Cornish accent, then plays him the AI audio to “prove” it. I don’t want to minimize the brilliance of Morgan’s deadpan performance or Brooker’s jokes, which approach the linguistic density of poetry and tend to contain sneaky insights that would be lost on the character giving voice to them. ( Marilyn Monroe , says Cunk, “effortlessly blended sex appeal, vulnerability, comic timing, and innocence into one irresistible package for men to destroy.”) Yet I suspect so many of us love to laugh at Cunk because, for once in this choose-your-own-facts decade, the joke is on the fool or cynic with outsize influence instead of on anyone fed up with the latter contingent’s misinformation and glibness and idiocy and self-promotion at any cost. There’s a difference between thoughtful questions and thoughtless ones, informed opinions and hysterical polemic, challenging authority on principle and mindless contrarianism for personal gain. And it’s a relief to be reminded that someone still knows it.

items.title: Gen X is in worse health than boomers – and I have a few theories as to why | Emma Beddington
items.summary: People in my age group are experiencing poorer physical and mental health than their elders at the same stage. Is this down to UPFs and booze, or something more complicated? I almost choked on my bird-food breakfast recently, reading that gen Xers are in worse health than boomers. Research by the UCL Centre for Longitudinal Studies , on approximately 8,000 participants aged about 50 from the 1970 British Cohort Study, found that my generation is experiencing “worse physical and mental health across adulthood than earlier-born generations”. Come on! How? We have better health education and pharmaceuticals than any previous generation, we’ve been browbeaten into cultivating our microbiomes and hitting our step counts, harassed to stand up (sitting’s worse than smoking!), jump around (protect your bones!) and pop creatine (unsure). Yet we’re still unhealthier than our elders?

items.originalTitle: Inside the Pentagon’s Failure to Shield U.S. Troops From Iranian Drones
items.author: Arash Khamooshi / Polaris / The New York Times
items.title: Inside the Pentagon’s Failure to Shield U.S. Troops From Iranian Drones
items.summary: F rom a distance , the Iranian drone resembled an arrowhead, pointing downward as it dove out of the sky. Its propeller, powered by the kind of motor typically used in dirt bikes and lawnmowers, produced a high-pitched wail. It struck midmorning on March 1, the second day of the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, hitting a logistics center in Kuwait used by the American military. Dozens of personnel from the Army Reserve were working at an office building there. The incoming drone, a variant of the Shahed, slammed through the roof of the building and detonated its payload. Six American service members were killed and more than two dozen wounded, several of them critically—the deadliest attack on U.S. troops in the war. It will be hard for the survivors to forget the drone’s distinctive noise. In Ukraine, which has faced years of attacks from this type of drone, people often compare its sound as it falls out of the sky to a Vespa revving its engine. But the noise no longer terrifies Ukrainians the way it once did. Last year, Ukraine’s arms industry developed a cheap and effective way to shoot down Shaheds. The U.S. military knew about this technology months before the war in Iran began. A group of senior American officers, worried about exactly the type of attack that killed those six soldiers in Kuwait, told me they repeatedly urged commanders in the Middle East to deploy the new Ukrainian technology. The Pentagon ignored their warnings, which included detailed reports sent up the chain of command. Several of the officers who tried to raise the alarm about Iranian Shaheds have since been fired or forced into early retirement. In a statement, the Pentagon disputed the officers’ account and said it was “disgusting” for the Atlantic to suggest that the U.S. military was “somehow unprepared” for the start of the war in Iran. “Central Command established the most extensive air defense umbrella in the world over the Middle East,” Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell wrote in the statement. “Make no mistake: The U.S. military has the best offensive and defensive capabilities of any nation on Earth, and we always protect our bases and our people.” The warnings were based on Ukraine’s experience with Russia, which acquired Shahed drones from Iran in 2022. Waves of them have pounded Ukrainian cities ever since, often in swarms of a few hundred per night. Last summer, the armed forces of Ukraine deployed a new type of interceptor to destroy Shaheds in midair. U.S. Army officers stationed in Germany began training on these interceptors that fall, and they asked their Ukrainian allies to produce a report about their new invention. The document, dated December 2025, was titled in the military’s turgid style: “Operational Experience in the Employment of UAV Interceptors in Countering Shahed-Type Aerial Threats.” It described in detail how Ukraine had developed these defensive weapons. A drawing of an interceptor appeared on the cover of the report, alongside a Shahed with a bull’s-eye on its belly. It was shared inside the military and with some U.S. allies in December, roughly two months before the war in Iran started. The Army’s European Command, led at the time by General Chris “C.D.” Donahue, had by then deployed the new interceptors at bases in Europe, including in Romania and Poland. Donahue and his team in Wiesbaden, Germany, urged their fellow officers to do the same at bases in other regions, especially in the Middle East, where the threat from Iranian drones seemed most obvious to them. The officers in Wiesbaden sent the document up to their commanders, and they pressed the leadership in Washington to act on it. Had their warnings been heeded, they believe the lives of U.S. soldiers could have been saved. Looking back, some of the officers still wonder whether they could have done more to protect those six Americans in Kuwait. “This should all have been figured out beforehand,” one of them told me. “How are we going to defend against Shaheds?” At the start of this year, the team of officers in Wiesbaden compiled a second report about the Ukrainian interceptors. To ensure the widest possible distribution, the military cleared it for public release in February. The document, roughly 12 pages long, described how European Command had fielded the Ukrainian interceptors at some of its bases. It offered detailed guidance for commanders in other regions to do the same. No one involved in preparing the two reports knew the timing of the U.S.-Israeli attack on Iran, which was then widely reported to be in the works. But they understood that any Iranian response would almost certainly involve Shahed drones, which the regime had invented, mass produced, and stockpiled. The second report was published on February 23, too late, as it turned out, for its warnings to make much difference. The war in Iran would start only five days later. [ Read: The glaring oversight in the U.S. war plan ] This account of the Pentagon’s failure to defend against these weapons is based on interviews with more than a dozen current and former military officers from the U.S. and Ukraine, who were involved in the effort to warn about the danger of Iranian drones and arm U.S. forces with the most effective countermeasures. Most of them spoke on condition of anonymity, because they fear reprisals from their commanders and officials at the Pentagon. Since taking office last year, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has overseen the widespread use of polygraph tests to find and punish military officers who speak with journalists without permission. He has also ordered the military to cut 20 percent of the positions reserved for generals and admirals across the armed forces. Donahue fell victim to that purge this summer. In the final months of his Army career, he worked with the team in Wiesbaden to send hundreds of Ukrainian interceptors to the Middle East, hoping they could defend against another deadly strike on U.S. forces. Hegseth did not support these efforts, the officers involved told me. “The technology is so effective. It’s so cheap,” one of them said. But the top officials in Washington did not want to accept it: “Because of arrogance, they said, Why do we need it? ” B y now , nearly five years after Russia invaded, most U.S. military officers would agree that Ukraine offers important lessons on the future of warfare. Its innovations in drone technology have been forged in the deadliest conflict Europe has seen in 80 years. Few American generals recognized their value sooner than Christopher Cavoli, who served until last year as the supreme allied commander of NATO. Roughly a year into the war, he hosted a training exercise with Ukrainian soldiers, and he was stunned by how quickly one of them, a private, figured out how to use a U.S.-military radar system. The soldier explained that, before volunteering to defend his country that year, he’d worked as professor of electrical engineering at a university in Kharkiv. “These guys were going to learn pretty quick,” Cavoli remembers thinking at the time. “They also worked all night,” he told me. “They didn’t take breaks.” By the second summer of the war, in 2023, the Ukrainians began to innovate in earnest, especially when it came to drone warfare. “That’s when we realized, Oh, these guys are doing stuff that we don’t do. Let’s go look at it seriously. ” About two years later, in the spring of 2025, NATO invited a team of drone operators from Ukraine to act as the enemy side—the red team—in a round of war games in Estonia. The blue team “took a whipping,” one of the American participants told me. The Ukrainians launched about 30 drone strikes in rapid succession, taking 17 armored vehicles and two NATO battalions out of the game before dinner. The U.S. troops were so unaccustomed to the red team’s tactics that some of them looked up at an incoming drone and waved their arms at its camera. One of the organizers of the drills later used that footage in a presentation to show how much the U.S. military had to learn. The Ukrainians also went home with a lesson. One of their commanders told me that the NATO troops, maneuvering around in their armored vehicles, had resembled a “golden-armored knight” who showed up for a gunfight with a fancy sword. “They are unable to accept reality,” he said. Drones now account for the great majority of casualties in the war. Ukraine’s military industry produced 4 million of them last year, far outpacing all NATO countries combined. [ Read: Inside the feud over Ukraine’s drone success ] That spring, I visited a company called Skyfall, whose factory in Kyiv could produce up to 4,000 small drones a day. Its founder led me through a maze of workshops and testing labs with hundreds of workers. Some of them flew drones through wind tunnels and pools of water to test their toughness. The best engineers, the founder told me, had been tasked with solving the problem of the Shaheds. The original design of the Shahed, with a propeller at the tail and a warhead at the tip, came from Iran in the first year of the war. But Russia soon began to manufacture its own Shaheds, adding new features to make them faster, more destructive, and harder to defeat. More than 6,000 of them were launched at Ukraine in the first 10 months of 2024. At first, Ukrainian soldiers tried to shoot them down with machine guns, using spotlights to scan the sky. Whenever possible, they also relied on advanced air-defense systems, such as the Patriot missile, which the U.S. and its allies provided to Ukraine in small batches. Patriots cost several million dollars per shot, and Ukraine needed to conserve them for bigger threats, such as Russian ballistic missiles. It could not afford to use them against drones that cost Russia roughly $35,000 each. For the engineers at Skyfall, the challenge came down to velocity. None of its drones could fly fast enough to catch Shaheds and ram them from behind. “We’ll get there,” the founder told me, scrolling through a series of grainy videos of his drones chasing Shaheds through the sky. “It’s definitely solvable.” Within a few months, several Ukrainian companies, including Skyfall, cracked the problem, developing a range of interceptors to take down Shaheds. They went by different names—Octopus, Sting, Bullet—but they had similar designs. Each one looked like a big thermos with rotors attached to its base and cost a few thousand dollars (much less than a Shahed, let alone a Patriot missile). They could be launched from an empty field or the back of a truck. To detect the interceptors’ targets, Ukraine also set up a network of acoustic sensors that listened for the noise of incoming Shaheds. The sensors did not require much engineering. Some were just smartphones affixed to long poles. When their mics picked up the sound of a Shahed, Ukraine’s air-defense forces sent up an interceptor to knock it down. The Ukrainian military purchased and deployed thousands of them last year. Before long, the interceptors had all but neutralized the threat, downing Shaheds at a rate of more than 90 percent, according to official estimates. U kraine’s allies took notice and started to spread the word. Last fall and winter, Skyfall gave frequent tours of its interceptor factory to Western officials. Some of the first visitors came from a command within the U.S. Army called Security Assistance Group Ukraine, or SAG-U. Headquartered in Wiesbaden, its officers work out of the recreation center at the base. Computer cables snake across the floor of their gym, beneath desks that stand on disused bowling lanes. Under a Pentagon order dating to the Biden administration, American generals rarely got permission to visit Ukraine; President Biden feared the Kremlin could view their presence as provocative. (It did not help that the first commander of SAG-U, General Antonio Aguto, resigned in 2024 after drinking too much at an official dinner in Kyiv. The Defense Department’s inspector general later found that he fell down drunk and injured his head.) But the Pentagon allowed other SAG-U officers to cycle through Ukraine on a regular basis. Aguto’s successor, General Curtis Buzzard, who had graduated from West Point in the same class as Donahue, made more than 30 trips to Ukraine. [ Read: Ukraine’s Dr. Strangelove ] The goals of such visits, apart from facilitating the delivery of U.S. weapons and intelligence, centered on the need for the U.S. military to draw lessons from Ukraine. Donahue would often tell his team that if they failed to study this war, “we would pay the price in blood and treasure.” Their hosts took the Americans to see Ukraine’s most innovative factories, drone units, and command posts. “Not everything they do is great,” one of the visiting officers told me. “But we need to know what we could leverage.” To codify and spread these insights, SAG-U and other teams in Wiesbaden began producing a variety of classified and unclassified reports that went out several times a week. The reports were meant to complement Donahue’s persistent efforts to impress the lessons of Ukraine onto the high command. Some of the briefing papers from Ukraine had a distribution list with more than 2,000 names, including officials and senior brass from allied nations. One group of officers at Wiesbaden, a rotating cast of Russia experts who called themselves the Troika, even wrote a book, How Russia Fights , to compile what they had learned. O f all Ukraine’s innovations , few if any looked as valuable and easy to replicate as the Shahed interceptors. By the time they appeared on the battlefield last summer, U.S. tensions with Iran had tipped into open warfare. The U.S. and Israel conducted a series of strikes in June 2025 against Iranian nuclear facilities. The response from Tehran did not leave the U.S. much reason to worry: Iran launched missiles at Israel and at a U.S. base in Qatar. American and allied air defenses, relying on the Patriot system, shot down the missiles heading for the base. At the White House and the Pentagon, the exchange fueled confidence that U.S. air power could defeat the Iranian regime with ease. Some inside the U.S. military, however, still saw it as prudent to prepare for Iran to escalate. Apart from its missile arsenal, Tehran had an enormous stockpile of Shaheds, many of them hidden underground beyond the reach of U.S. air strikes. They were cheap and plentiful enough for Iran to overwhelm the U.S. supply of Patriots and other sophisticated air defenses. Their range of potential targets included every U.S. base in the Middle East, and they could threaten any ship passing through the Strait of Hormuz, the aorta of the global oil supply. Deploying cheap interceptors to help defeat these weapons seemed like an obvious move. By the end of last year, Donahue had already integrated them into the forces under his command in Europe. The U.S. Army officers in Wiesbaden urged their colleagues in the Middle East to do the same. “It’s just common sense,” a person familiar with their deployment told me. None of the officers in Wiesbaden ever received a clear explanation of why the Trump administration ignored this advice. But the officers sensed two reasons behind the resistance in Washington: arrogance and politics. During their clash in the Oval Office in February 2025, Trump told Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that Ukraine did not have any cards to play. The encounter set a new tone for their relationship, and it sent a signal within the Trump administration that Ukraine should be treated as a supplicant, not an ally. At the Pentagon, “Hegseth did not want to hear the word Ukraine ,” a senior Ukrainian official told me of that period. U.S. Army officers in Europe sensed a similar toxicity. If you brought up Ukraine at the Pentagon, “if you were lucky, you were met with a sneer,” one of them told me. Under the Biden administration, Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin received weekly updates from SAG-U about the war. Once Hegseth took over, those briefings stopped. So did nearly all U.S. military aid to Ukraine. [ Read: Dan Driscoll’s parting shot ] Ukraine’s most vocal advocate at the top of the Trump administration turned out to be Dan Driscoll, the U.S. Army secretary. During a visit to Wiesbaden in the spring of 2025, Driscoll got a detailed briefing from Donahue about Ukrainian weapons systems. “A light bulb went off,” he later said of that experience. Driscoll, a former Army officer, was particularly impressed with the command-and-control software known as Delta, which Ukraine developed to process data from the war zone, including the acoustic sensors that pick up the sound of incoming Shaheds. The system provides an interactive map that soldiers could use to monitor the battlefield and react in real time. Nine months after his visit to Wiesbaden, Driscoll joined forces with Donahue and others to establish the U.S. Army’s first experimental drone unit, the Unmanned Assault Battalion. Composed of roughly 600 soldiers stationed in Italy, the unit had orders to work with Ukrainian advisers in developing advanced drones and the means to counter them. Around that time, Zelensky and Trump began negotiating a deal for the U.S. to purchase Ukraine’s most advanced military equipment. “The people of America need this technology, and you need to have it in your arsenal,” Zelensky told the New York Post . But after a few rounds of talks, the U.S. shelved the deal last fall. That decision came down to American hubris, one of the Ukrainian officials involved in the negotiations told me at the time. The message from the White House amounted to this, he said: “Know your place. We have the greatest military in the world. We don’t need anything from you.” T hat attitude changed when the war with Iran started. In the first days of March, Zelensky received a flood of calls from U.S. allies in the Middle East. They wanted to know about Ukrainian interceptors, and how many of them Zelensky could sell in a hurry. The previous week, U.S. and Israeli air strikes managed to kill much of Iran’s leadership. But Iran’s arsenal of missiles and drones allowed it to stay in the fight far longer than Trump expected. Its response featured a barrage of Shahed drones, by some estimates more than 2,000, aimed at targets across the Middle East: military bases, airports, and logistics hubs used by the Americans, as well as civilian targets and infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Bahrain, the United Arab Emirates, and elsewhere in the region. In trying to shoot down the drones, the U.S. and its allies quickly burned through most of their supply of Patriot missiles. In some cases, such as with the Shahed strike on the base in Kuwait, U.S. air defenses failed—with deadly consequences. One of the survivors of that strike, Lieutenant Colonel Tim Halbur, recalled waking up in the wreckage of his office, his uniform covered in blood, and the bones of his right elbow falling away. One of his comrades, Major Stephen Ramsbottom, later told the Associated Press that the base should have been better defended. “This type of fight has been going on for five years in Ukraine, and our excuse is we didn’t expect it to happen to us,” he said. “That’s preposterous in my mind.” When the team in Wiesbaden heard about the attack, they did their best to prevent another one. Donahue gathered a few hundred of the Ukrainian interceptors deployed under his command in Europe, and he sent them to U.S. bases in the Persian Gulf. The general also drafted and signed a series of confidential requests to the leadership in Kyiv, including to Zelensky’s office, asking for more interceptors, according to three people familiar with the documents. [ Read: Building tanks while the Ukrainians master drones ] His counterparts in Kyiv feared it would cost Donahue his job. “I was asking him: Aren’t you afraid to be signing that?” one of them told me. Given the tensions between Trump and Zelensky, the Ukrainians wondered whether Donahue’s efforts could result in a backlash from the White House. “He said: I don’t care. I just want to help some American soldiers . ” (Donahue declined to comment.) The Ukrainians were also eager to help, in part to show their gratitude for years of U.S. support. On the sixth day of the war, Zelensky announced that Ukraine would send equipment and experts to the Middle East to help the U.S. counter Iranian drones. Trump seemed open to the arrangement. In an interview with Reuters, he declared the same day that he would accept “any assistance from any country.” But his position flipped a week later. “No, we don’t need their help in drone defense,” Trump said on Fox News Radio on March 13. “We know more about drones than anybody. We have the best drones in the world, actually.” Without a clear signal from Trump, the team in Wiesbaden sensed, the Pentagon did not want to accept Ukrainian assistance. “It’s the politics,” one of them told me. “If I’m Hegseth, I don’t know where Trump sits with Ukraine day to day. So I don’t necessarily want to go all in.” Only Driscoll seemed willing to stick his neck out. In early March, the Army secretary placed a call to Eric Schmidt, a former CEO of Google who has invested in Ukraine’s defense industry. Schmidt’s drone company had worked with Skyfall to produce an interceptor called the Merops, which had been effective against Shaheds in Ukraine. Within days, Schmidt and Driscoll managed to ship 13,000 of them on chartered flights to the Middle East. They believed the interceptors would be useful in reopening the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran had begun attacking ships with drones and missiles. The mission was an almost total failure. According to two people familiar with its outcome, the Merops shot down only one Iranian Shahed. The reason for the flop came down to poor planning, these people told me. Host countries in the Middle East had never operated these weapons, and they were slow to approve their deployment. Schmidt fumed over the bureaucratic delays, his associates told me. He knew they would likely translate into more lives lost to Shahed strikes and further disruption to trade through the Strait of Hormuz. The Merops deployment also faced a technical problem that could not be solved in a matter of days. Without the network of sensors that Ukraine uses to identify incoming drones, the interceptors could not find and follow their targets. “We screwed it up,” a senior Ukrainian official involved in that operation told me. Some of the officers in Wiesbaden wondered whether they could have made their arguments more forcefully to the Pentagon or to their counterparts in the Middle East. Looking back on the deaths at the base in Kuwait, “you want to know you did everything you could,” one of them told me. Then again, the officer added, “I pushed and pushed and pushed, but nobody was really pulling.” Instead, the Pentagon continued its cull of the upper ranks, and it gutted the team in Wiesbaden. Donahue relinquished his command in early July, about a year after his boss, Cavoli, had done the same. The general Hegseth promoted to lead the Army, Christopher LaNeve, announced in August that the specialized drone unit Donahue helped create, the Unmanned Assault Battalion, would be dismantled. LaNeve described the decision as part of a “back to basics” approach. Other generals seethed over the move in private, while both Democrats and Republicans on Capitol Hill denounced it publicly. “It hurts our ability to acquire the critical knowledge and skills that can be gained from working with and learning from Ukrainian soldiers,” a group of four lawmakers wrote in a letter to Driscoll and LaNeve on September 1. The next day, Driscoll stepped down after 18 months as Army secretary. Buzzard, the SAG-U commander, had announced his retirement about a month before. I n early September , I paid a visit to the base in Wiesbaden, hoping to see what was left of the teams created to learn from the war in Ukraine. They seemed to be in a state of mourning. At the entrance to their base, seven portraits of the base commanders hung on the wall. In the frame on the left, Donahue’s portrait had been replaced with a black square. From their desks in the recreation center, the officers of SAG-U continued to gather intelligence and put out their reports. Their new commander, who took over in early August, did not grant them permission to speak with me. But several officers agreed to sit down in Wiesbaden and discuss the war in Ukraine. Their main concern at the time related to a new type of drone that Russia began using this spring, a souped-up version of the Shahed equipped with a jet engine, which allows it to fly much faster than Ukraine’s interceptors. Hundreds of these new drones had been hammering Kyiv and other cities for weeks, killing scores of civilians and devastating the infrastructure needed to keep the lights on and the economy running. [ Read: The new subterranean front ] The team in Wiesbaden described the new Shaheds as a fiendish challenge, requiring an entirely new interceptor. Some of them doubted whether Ukrainian engineers could produce one by winter. But soon after, two of Ukraine’s leading drone manufacturers, including Skyfall, said they had found a solution. Zelensky announced in late September that Ukraine had deployed an interceptor capable of defeating jet-powered Shaheds. In the Middle East, Iran has already used this weapon against U.S. forces, which have relied on Patriot missiles, fighter jets, and other sophisticated hardware to shoot them down. Ukraine appears close to a much more efficient solution. But the U.S. has no deal to buy this new generation of interceptors. For the officers in Wiesbaden, it looked like a sign that the Pentagon could make the same mistake twice: ignoring the latest innovations and, in the process, putting the lives of its troops in danger. Eight months after the deadly strike in Kuwait, the U.S military has still not deployed the sort of network of sensors and interceptors Ukraine uses against Shaheds. According to the latest estimates, the U.S. has used up nearly three-quarters of its Patriot missiles since the start of the war in Iran. Replenishing that stockpile will take years . In the meantime, U.S. soldiers in the Middle East are staying close to their air-raid shelters, keeping their ears pricked for the whine of inbound drones.

items.originalTitle: The ultimate adulting task: signing up for health insurance
items.author: Blake Farmer, Cara Anthony, KFF Health News
items.title: The ultimate adulting task: signing up for health insurance
items.summary: Not many 22-year-olds share DJ Mikunda’s enthusiasm for health insurance coverage. “You know what sounds like a good Friday night? It’s looking at health insurance,” he joked. But Mikunda has a reason to be eager. He has gone without coverage since he left home and started working in 2023. He’s now a manager at a gas station in St. Louis. In years past, he has looked at plans on the health insurance marketplace at healthcare.gov — but the options proved overwhelming and a bit too expensive. “I feel like I’m a well-informed individual,” Mikunda said. “I try to stay updated on what a deductible is and what the premiums are and copays. And I’m still finding myself a little bit lost.” To sort through the basics, HealthQ introduced Mikunda to independent assister Jackie Shrago , who has been helping people navigate the insurance marketplace since the early days of the Affordable Care Act. The QTip: Search for a free “independent assister” on healthcare.gov to better understand your insurance options. Income Drives the Conversation Shrago started by asking Mikunda about his income. How much money you expect to make in the coming year determines whether you’re eligible for reduced monthly payments. The system uses a sliding scale for households making less than 400% of the federal poverty rate — which means, for 2027 enrollees, an individual with no children can make up to $63,480 and still qualify for a discount. A person in their mid-20s making $50,000, for instance, would get an average 23% discount, according to KFF’s subsidy calculator . For someone making $30,000, the tax credit would cover nearly three-quarters of the cost. It’s important to estimate next year’s income as accurately as possible. If you end up making more than anticipated, you may owe money back to the government. “The last thing you want is a surprise when you file your income taxes,” Shrago told Mikunda. Short-Term Affordability vs. Long-Term Needs Then, Shrago pivoted to the other considerations: How much can you afford to pay every month? And what kind of coverage do you really need? It’s a personal decision about financial planning and risk tolerance, balancing up-front payments with out-of-pocket costs. Mikunda knows he’ll need regular doctor visits and prescription medication, because he has a chronic joint condition that has gone virtually untreated since he started working and lost Medicaid coverage. So he might consider stretching his monthly budget for a plan that covers more of the medical cost. Those financial trade-offs drive much of the decision, forcing you to find a “comfortable medium” between the level of coverage you want and the amount you’re willing to pay, Mikunda said. Gather Your Decision Team There’s much to consider, especially for a first-timer. But one-on-one help is available at healthcare.gov . If you click on the link to “ Find local help ,” you can filter specifically to search for “independent assisters” like Shrago in your ZIP code. Unlike insurance agents and brokers, assisters are forbidden from charging for their services or receiving compensation from insurance companies. (The brokers listed at healthcare.gov far outnumber the independent assisters, but the assisters are findable.) Shrago also recommends starting the selection process early enough to step away and think. “If you’re dealing with something that is uncertain enough and you feel really awkward about it, you don’t need to make a decision today,” she said. “Take your time and think about it.” Assisters tend to have the least availability right before the federal marketplace’s Jan. 15 deadline, so reach out early. People and Policy The Trump administration cut funding for independent assisters and navigator nonprofits by roughly 90% in 2025. When making that announcement, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services said the program was inefficient , costing more than $1,000 per person enrolled. The reduction in funding means fewer people helping. In Ohio, for example, the number of paid navigators serving state residents dropped from 50 to five at the start of open enrollment in 2025. Katherine Ruppelt and Emily Siner at Nashville Public Radio contributed to this report. items.summary: High-profile crimes and disease outbreaks obscure the fact that the big ships are largely safe – and seeing record numbers of bookings This month, there has been a swell of stories about things going wrong on cruises. A man was arrested in Texas after he allegedly killed a woman during a voyage through the Caribbean. A pianist on a Royal Caribbean cruise from California was rescued by two fishers in the Pacific Ocean after he went overboard. And Singapore seized the MV Odyssey, a US-operated cruise ship that was supposed to offer retirees a “permanent” life at sea. The operator ran out of money because of increased fuel prices and dropped all its passengers off in Cambodia.

items.originalTitle: Gen Z believes using AI is making their colleagues dumb and lazy—but may paradoxically see it as key to their own promotion, Wharton says
items.author: Sasha Rogelberg
items.title: Gen Z believes using AI is making their colleagues dumb and lazy—but may paradoxically see it as key to their own promotion, Wharton says
items.summary: Last year, researchers from Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon University revealed startling evidence about the impact of using AI on how—and how hard—people think, finding that among more than 300 knowledge workers, leaning too much on AI tools like ChatGPT was associated with diminished critical thinking skills . The study, mirrored by results from MIT-led research , suggested that even using AI for low-stakes tasks such as proofreading “can lead to significant negative outcomes in high-stakes contexts,” like writing legal documents, the study authors wrote. For the young generation of digital natives navigating AI anxiety around keeping up with peers using the technology and AI displacing them from jobs, the fear of the technology making people dumber is dominant. But that hasn’t stopped them from using AI—even when they’re explicitly told not to. A Wharton-led survey published earlier this year, conducted in partnership with Gallup and the Walton Family Foundation, found young people are ramping up their AI use, even as their concerns about it causing lazy thinking persist. A survey of nearly 2,500 U.S. adults between the ages of 18 and 28 completed in October 2025 found 79% of respondents believed AI makes people lazier, and 62% said they had concerns it makes people less smart. “What we find is deep ambivalence on how Gen Z is thinking [about] using AI,” Benjamin Lira Luttges, a postdoctoral scholar at Wharton who led research for the report, told Fortune . Despite these fears, Gen Zers have increased their AI usage. Pew Research Center data published in June found 66% of people ages 18 to 29 have ever used an AI chatbot, such as ChatGPT, up from 55% in 2024. However, 37% of those young adults said they believed the impact of AI on them over the next 20 years would be negative, the most pessimistic attitude of any age group surveyed. The paradox of Gen Z’s willingness to use AI at the office, even amid persistent worries about the technology’s impact on critical thinking, lays bare the young generation’s complicated feelings toward AI, according to the report’s authors. After all, Gen Z’s fraught relationship with AI runs deep. Nearly one-fifth of the generation is worried about AI displacing them at work, yet they lead the workplace in AI adoption . Though they require some decoding, Gen Z’s tangled attitudes toward AI can be critical in designing a path forward for the technology, more broadly, to be best integrated into the workplace, Lira Luttges suggested. “Young people lead the adoption of new technologies, and a lot of things that are often seen as fringe, as not mainstream, are adopted by young people and eventually become part of the mainstream,” he said. “So in a sense … looking at Gen Z is a way of looking towards the future of work.” What are Gen Z’s fraught feelings toward AI? Lira Luttges speculates the biggest mental factor informing Gen Z’s attitudes toward AI is simply a bias toward immediate gratification , a disposition more prominent in younger, developing minds. “There’s a legitimate tradeoff between benefits and costs that you get from using AI,” he said. “Our brains are wired to prefer smaller, immediate rewards versus long-term, delayed rewards.” As Gen Z grapples with finding or keeping jobs, as well as scaling their career ladders, job performance bolstered by an AI boost may hold more appeal than the less tangible threat of critical thinking skills loss. Similarly, even if an employer does not want an employee using AI for certain tasks, those workers, particularly if young, might consider getting their tasks done efficiently as more important, particularly if the risk of getting caught is slow, Lira Luttges noted. Anyone—not just Gen Z—could also fall victim to the better-than-average effect , a statistically impossible phenomenon of most people generally believing they are above average at a certain task. Gen Z survey respondents, for example, may see themselves as AI power-users, Lira Luttges said. Sure, AI could atrophy critical thought capabilities and make other people lazy, but not those filling out the survey. How will Gen Z shape the future of work? To maximize how AI is used in the workplace, employers should not ban AI, but rather embrace ambivalence toward it, the report authors argued. According to the survey, respondents who reported using AI more frequently worried less about its impact on intelligence and motivation, indicating AI anxiety may resolve over time. But resolving AI anxiety doesn’t address the question of AI use impacting critical thought. Some future-of-work experts, including Mark Beasley, professor and director at North Carolina State University’s Poole College of Management, believe a critical thinking gap, not an AI skills gap, will pose a serious threat to organizational pipelines and business operations. Beasley told Fortune the threat AI poses to entry-level jobs could mean insufficient training and experience for middle- and eventually upper-tier positions in the near future. “The biggest risk organizations face is just being stagnant,” he said. But as long as workplaces are intentional about how they implement AI, Lira Luttges said the technology won’t have a significant impact on critical thinking. “For every task, there are two kinds of efforts,” Lira Luttges said. “There is effort that is germane to the task, that is intrinsic to the thing that you’re doing, and that kind of effort is the effort that you put in, and gets translated into learning. But there’s a lot of effort that is just there, that’s just like friction, that doesn’t really teach you anything.” “You should outsource the crap, not the craft,” he added. A version of this story was published on Fortune.com on Jan., 30 2026. items.originalTitle: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.author: Melissa Denes
items.title: ‘She was a monster’: the real Patricia Highsmith, by the people who knew her
items.summary: A new film starring Helen Mirren explores the Ripley writer’s later years, but was she really so rude and eccentric? Editors and publishers who worked with her look back Publisher and bookseller Otto Penzler has loved Patricia Highsmith’s work all his life, but their first meeting was a washout. In 1984, she agreed to give a reading at The Mysterious Bookshop, his store on West 56th Street in New York. The American author of the Ripley novels, then 63, had lived in Europe for 20 years – in England, then France, then Switzerland – and seldom made public appearances, so he had high hopes. “But no one showed up. We had maybe four people,” Penzler says from his book-lined office under the shop. Now 84, with a tidy white beard and a warm, amused manner, he is just back from a crime fiction convention and still very much in the game. Highsmith, he recalls, had little time for her readers. “She was somewhat taciturn. People got their book signed and left within five minutes. I had a two-hour event scheduled, so what does one do? With some authors, I can say, ‘Let me buy you dinner.’ Well, not with Pat.” She stonewalled his small talk about France with an “I can’t stand the bloody frogs”.

items.originalTitle: Reclaiming Mary Cassatt: putting overlooked American artist back at heart of impressionism
items.author: Kim Willsher in Paris
items.title: Reclaiming Mary Cassatt: putting overlooked American artist back at heart of impressionism
items.summary: New exhibition restores painter’s place as leading figure in French movement that revolutionised art As a painter, friend, and collaborator of Edgar Degas, who exhibited with impressionist artists including Claude Monet and Camille Pissarro, Mary Cassatt was at the heart of the 19th-century movement that emerged in France and revolutionised art. She was also a woman and foreign – “American, American through and through” is how she described herself. As a result, in the 100 years since her death, Cassatt has been frequently overlooked in the country where she produced her best work.
